To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Gd-CA with low stability (linear and non-ionic) are associated with NSF; (2) the stability of GAd-CA is an important factor in determining their propensity to induce NSF; and (3) macrocyclic G-CA of high stability are not associated with NSF.

NSF is a rare fibrosing disorder which is more likely to occur in patients with renal insufficiency and in those who receive linear Gd3+-based contrast agents (linear Gd-CA), especially the linear non-ionic chelates, gadodiamide, and gadoversetamine, than any other linear or macrocycic Gd3+-CA.
NSF is a rare but serious complication of Gd-based contrast agents.

NSF is a rare but potentially fatal disease and that the use of gadodiamide should be restricted in the patients with advanced reduction in renal functions, and that the use and the stability of Gda-CA are important factors in the pathogenesis.
NSF is caused by the use of linear or non-ionic gadolinium-based contrast agents, especially gadodiamide, in patients with advanced reduction of renal function.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NSF is a disease of fibrocytes and that the fibrogenic potential of gadolinium ions is dependent on the chemical stability of the Gd-CA.
the stability of the Gd-CA, and the consequent transmetallation of free gadolinium ions in the body, is a key factor in the pathophysiology and prevention of NSF.
the stability of GAd-CA is a major factor in the pathophysiology and that macrocyclic GAd-CA of high stability are the safest for patients with renal failure and are unlikely to cause NSF.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of Gd-DOTA, the most stable agent, is the safest option in patients with severe renal impairment.
the stability of Gda-based contrast agents is a key factor in the development of nephrogenic systemic fibroses.
the use of Gd-DA and Gd-DTPA should be avoided in patients with severe renal impairment.
